title: Continual Learning through Control Minimization
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Backprop-based regularizers keep drifting and fail to converge on prior tasks, while the curvature-aware dynamical approach converges and stays stable.
layout: 2 panels (a, b), each with two line plots; dashed vertical line marks Task B 90% accuracy
description: A light teal background holds two grouped panels, a and b, each with two line plots over training steps on Task B (0 to 1000). Panel a shows Task A loss increase on the left and Task A accuracy decrease on the right. Four colored curves appear: BP in light orange, EWC in orange, FISH in dark red, and EFC in green. A legend pairs each method with a Fisher matrix symbol (I, F^D, F, F-tilde). BP and EWC keep rising. FISH and EFC plateau, and EFC stays lowest on accuracy decrease. Panel b shows Class-IL loss on the left and Class-IL accuracy on the right. BP, EWC and FISH drift toward worse values, while the green EFC curve converges to low loss and high accuracy. A dashed vertical line marks Task B reaching 90% accuracy. A dotted inset on the accuracy plot shows a gradient-norm parabola diagram.
caption: Empirical validation of the learning theory. (a) Task A loss increase as a function of training on Task B, the dynamical approximation of the full Fisher $\tilde{F}$ follows the analytical full Fisher $F$ (left). The Task A accuracy decrease is less for the EFC method than the full Fisher (right). (b) Class-IL loss (left) and accuracy (left) do not converge for any backpropagation-based regularization method and do converge for the EFC method.
abstract: Catastrophic forgetting remains a fundamental challenge for neural networks when tasks are trained sequentially. In this work, we reformulate continual learning as a control problem where learning and preservation signals compete within neural activity dynamics. We convert regularization penalties into preservation signals that protect prior-task representations. Learning then proceeds by minimizing the control effort required to integrate new tasks while competing with the preservation of prior tasks. At equilibrium, the neural activities produce weight updates that implicitly encode the full prior-task curvature, a property we term the continual-natural gradient, requiring no explicit curvature storage. Experiments confirm that our learning framework recovers true prior-task curvature and enables task discrimination, outperforming existing methods on standard benchmarks without replay.
